sentences.text: Aquilolamna milarcae, known as the eagle shark, possessed a torpedo-shaped body with extremely long, winglike pectoral fins that were 1.90 meters wide.
These expansive fins were wider than the animal's total body length of 1.65 meters.
The fossil specimen was collected and prepared by local teacher Margarito González González.
The description was controversial because the authors claimed the fossil was in a public museum, but it was actually in the private collection of politician Mauricio Fernández Garza.
Aquilolamna was described from a single well-preserved specimen recovered in 2012 from Vallecillo in the state of Nuevo León, Mexico, and the species was formally described in 2021.
Researchers hypothesize that Aquilolamna was a planktivorous filter-feeder with a manta ray-like body plan, a trait suggesting convergent evolution.
The Agua Nueva Formation where Aquilolamna was found is thought to consist of sediments deposited on the outer edge of a shallow continental shelf.

Aquilolamna belongs to the class Chondrichthyes and is classified in its own family, Aquilolamnidae, which is tentatively assigned to the mackerel sharks. It was tentatively assigned to the order Lamniformes based on morphological similarities to other members of that family.
Aquilolamna lived between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago during the Turonian stage.

The authors of the description were accused of scientific colonialism for failing to collaborate with local paleontologists, which is mandated by Mexico's national regulatory agency. Other paleontologists have reservations about classifying Aquilolamna within Lamniformes due to its unusual features, suggesting future research is needed. It is suspected that Aquilolamna may be closely allied with Cretomanta, an extinct shark of uncertain taxonomic affinity.
